Taxi Drones

By: John Webb | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We get a glimpse into the future of urban travel where roads become obsolete, as driver-less taxis take to the heavens in crash-free, pollution-free sky-ways.

Unique Selling Point:
Germany is fast becoming the epicentre of future transport engineering. Munich, Frankfurt, Cologne... all are home to companies working on secret projects aimed at solving the mounting urban mobility crisis. Growing city populations, congested roads and pollution have caused a major re-think around how we transport people safely, economically and in massive numbers. One solution is tapping into drone technology to develop crash-proof taxis capable of ferrying people across cities in double-quick time. Carte Blanche visits Germany, the epicentre of modern European engineering, to see first hand the cutting edge concepts taking us closer to a roadless world.

Summary:
Airbus Industries is best known as one of the two biggest global aircraft manufacturers. Its most iconic contribution to modern aviation being the massive A380 superjet. But, behind closed doors at a facility on the outskirts of Munich, the company has a team dedicated to delivering groundbreaking design in the field of unmanned flight. The team is headed up by South African, Jana Rosenmann, a commerce and international relations expert. One of their civil functions (they also have a military mandate) is to develop pilot-less - or autonomous - passenger drones. In conjunction with other multi-national corporations, such as Audi, significant progress has already been made. Airbus also has units in other parts of the world working on similar concepts.

Meanwhile, across town, at the headquarters of Lilium, similar strides are being made with an equally impressive team of engineers but on far smaller budgets. This aeronautical start-up has already attracted significant investment, and has tested a vertical take-off and landing, autonomous craft capable of travelling at 300km per hour.

Carte Blanche would visit both facilities for a detailed look at the latest in autonomous flight technology being developed by a multinational powerhouse on the one hand, and a slick, modern upstart on the other. Both are bringing the future to within touching distance.

Further information:
While South Africa maintains an impressive presence in the global technological landscape given its resources, it has yet to join the autonomous flight race. However, there will doubtless be transport or engineering experts able to shed light on how this technology would benefit SA and other developing countries.

Extra Budget Items:
Return flights ex Dublin and London for John Webb and cameraman (tbc) as well as one night's accommodation and transfers (trains and Uber or car hire). There is likely to be an excess baggage cost for the cameraman.

Press Release:


Taxi Drones
There are more than a billion cars on our roads globally and with millions more added every year, our planet is increasingly congested and polluted. Now, engineers are turning to an impressive mixture of drone technology and artificial intelligence to find a real solution for the future. Could self-piloted flying taxis help solve the urban mobility crisis and save our cities?


Script:


2nd Revised Script: CB Taxi Drones.

Footage: Volocopter 2011 First Manned Flight (VC1 2011)

Text: Somewhere in southern Germany, 2011.

VO (22”): This is a German man, sitting on a flying Yoga ball covered in a towel.
It is the world’s first manned flight of an electric multi-copter and lasts for exactly 90 seconds. It might not look it, but this is a little piece of history, a significant step in trying to solve one of the biggest crises of the modern age.

Link: The first truly mass produced vehicle rolled off the assembly line in 1908. Today, there are around 1.1 billion cars on the road with – according to most estimates – more than 70 million added every year. That means, in the time it’s taken me to tell you about that stat – 20 seconds - another 44 cars have been made.

VO: At this rate, there’ll be 2 billion cars on the road by 2040. And you can imagine what that will do to the rush hour commute.

Link: So, here then the provision list for surviving peak hour traffic: you have a sandwich, some fruit, something to keep you hydrated and if like me you’re over 45 then a CD for nostalgic reasons and… bucket loads of patience.

VO: Each year we’re spending 160 hours in peak hour traffic. That’s a week of our lives cooped up in our cars. It’s a frustration Air Traffic specialist, Arthur Bradshaw, who lives on Johannesburg’s East Rand, knows all too well.

Upsound Arthur Bradshaw: (00:20:41:01) If I’ve got to go to Sandton from here in the mornings for a meeting, I have to leave two hours before. Takes me two hours to get home, that’s nuts. If I can have nice little bubble I can climb into, programme it and off it goes, it’s going to be as fast as the Gautrain.

VO: Well, Carte Blanche travelled to Germany to meet some people who are planning exactly that.

Upsound Alex Zosel: (00070 @ 2:18 to 2:30) I needed an hour or two, I had crazy ideas and I think two weeks later I had the first idea of taxi flying and mass transportation.

VO: When Alex Zosel was urged to join a revolution in how we get from A to B, he jumped at the chance. He co-founded a start-up company called Volocopter – the people behind the flying yoga ball.

Upsound Alex Zosel: (00070 @ 2:32 to 2:43) It was obvious to me what the advantage of this type of technology compared to a normal type of helicopter that would open-up a completely new type of flying, a new kind of mobility.

Footage: Volocopter March, 2016 First Manned VR2 Flight (Bemannter Erstflug NC)

Text: Germany, March 2016

VO: In 2016, Zosel himself took the controls of what’s known in these circles as an Electric Vertical Take-Off and Landing craft or eVTOL – although you can think of it as the yoga ball’s younger, more athletic cousin. At one point, Zosel felt confident enough to let go of the joystick and applaud his colleagues below.

Upsound Alex Zosel: (00072 @ 9:43 to 10:08) That was only a thank you to the technicals because everybody could do that flight. My mother, who was just 80 years old, also flew this aircraft with a joystick, but she’s sitting on a chair outside with the same joystick. So, it’s really, really easy.

VO: Easy perhaps, but that’s only half the battle. To fully realise the urban mobility revolution, these craft are going to be autonomous. In other words, they’re going to have to fly themselves. Science fiction, surely? Well, not according to Zosel.

Upsound Alex Zosel: (00074 @ 5:57 to 6:20) In 2004 you don’t have a mobile phone with navigation, you have your paper to find your way with a car and you stop and ask people where’s the bar I want to go… and that’s 2004, 14 years ago. And you see how fast things are coming and the Technik is here now.

VO: And, with the technology already at their fingertips, companies like Volocopter have a rather exciting vision of the very near future:

(Footage Volocopter User Story)

VO: This could one day be how many of us travel within our cities – ok, perhaps without the designer suits and fancy cars. A taxi hailing app – no different from the ones we’re already using – putting us in touch with a fully autonomous, invisible highway in the sky; slower and at lower altitudes than commercial jets, but faster, cleaner and more efficient than cars. All for the price of a bus or train ride.

(Pause)

Before we reach that Utopian future, though, it’s all about testing, testing and more testing.

(Footage Vahana First Flight)

Vahana is an eVTOL project by the aeronautics giant, Airbus. It’s being engineered in the United States, and while it’s driven by a major multi-national, its roots are just as humble as the Volocopter’s.

(Pause)

In January this year, it flew all on its own for the very first time. Not bad for a concept that was nothing more than a drawing on a napkin just two years ago.

(Pause)

(Footage Jana Rosenmann exterior establisher)

VO: South African, Jana Rosenmann (pronounced Ro-zen-mann), is an executive at Airbus. We met her at the corporation’s Defence and Space division, outside Munich where she heads up Unmanned Aerial Systems. Coming up with the technology, she says, is only part of the challenge.

Upsound Jana Rosenmann: (00015 @ 5:22 to 5:37) The areas where we are flying drones today are not regulated. The areas where we have commercial and military aircraft flying, this is regulated. But here we’re talking about a much lower altitude level and there’s just no blue book, it doesn’t exist.

VO: So, while the engineers do their thing, this Commerce graduate from Wits University admits there’s still lots to do before the regulation people give the go ahead to flying taxis – especially ones not flown by humans.

Upsound Jana Rosenmann: (00015 @ 3:01 to 3:12) We need to win confidence with the regulatory bodies, we need to win confidence also with the general-public. Because there is a perception that people aren’t just going to jump into an autonomous air vehicle.

(Footage Vahana Video Final)

VO: A good place to start are the eVTOLS design benefits such as their multiple rotors: if one stops working there are others to do the job. Throw in the latest radar and satellite technology and safety starts looking like less of a problem than you’d imagine.

VO: Ultimately, though, if air taxis are going to become a reality, we’ll be handing over our lives to intelligent computers – not only on board, but in the systems directing air traffic too.

(Footage Vahana Video Final @ 0:44 – please title Airbus Sense and Avoid Tech)

Upsound Arthur Bradshaw: (28:54:05) When you get these autonomous vehicles as you call it, they going to be very self-sustained and very full of intelligence, which we call artificial intelligence and able to actually determine what does the separation require between me and this other vehicle whether it is a piloted vehicle or an unpiloted vehicle because they’re all part of the system and all of those things are going to be talking to each other.

John Webb Question: (00021 @ 4:29) Where do you stand on artificial intelligence because it is a controversial field?

Upsound Jana Rosenmann: (00016 @0:25 to :043) Honestly, if we want to move to autonomy and automated systems, the human being can’t do that, it’s going to have to be aided by machines. So, if it’s our end goal to move to automated systems, we have to have machine learning, we have to have AI, because there’s just no other way to do it.

Link: Our skies are already used by commercial and private planes, helicopters, and remotely piloted drones, so you’d be forgiven for thinking that adding hundreds of autonomous flying taxis to our airspace will replace one type of gridlock with another.

VO: Actually, our airspace is still relatively empty, and in many ways provides a blank canvass. So, the innovation trying to turn us all into low altitude commuters is continuing at breakneck speed.

(Footage 2017-10-24 Volocopter Image Clip) and Italdesign Pop Up 2018)

VO: Volocopter has already taken to the air in Dubai in the first ever public demonstration of an autonomous urban taxi;

(Italdesign Pop Up 2018)

and Airbus is now exploring ways of bringing together two dimensions: land and air. The future, it seems, is within reach.

Ends.

In conjunction with other multi-national corporations, such as Audi, significant progress has already been made. Airbus also has units in other parts of the world working on similar concepts. Meanwhile, across town, at the headquarters of Lilium, similar strides are being made with an equally impressive team of engineers but on far smaller budgets. This aeronautical start-up has already attracted significant investment, and has tested a vertical take-off and landing, autonomous craft capable of travelling at 300km per hour. Carte Blanche would visit both facilities for a detailed look at the latest in autonomous flight technology being developed by a multinational powerhouse on the one hand, and a slick, modern upstart on the other. Both are bringing the future to within touching distance.
metadata.Further information: While South Africa maintains an impressive presence in the global technological landscape given its resources, it has yet to join the autonomous flight race. However, there will doubtless be transport or engineering experts able to shed light on how this technology would benefit SA and other developing countries.
